title: The Most Ridiculous Wars in History

beats.say: In November 1932, the Australian army rolled into the wheat fields of Western Australia with two machine guns and ten thousand rounds of ammunition.
Their enemy was fast, fearless, about six feet tall, and covered in feathers.
Right, lads. How hard can it be?
Spoiler: very hard.
And that's not even the only ridiculous war in history.
Today we're counting down seven ridiculous wars, fought over a kettle, a bucket, an ear, a pig and, yes, emus.

show.text: The Most Ridiculous Wars in History
show.sub: Seven wars. All real. Well, mostly.

beats.say: Number seven: the Kettle War of 1784.
Quick setup: for about two hundred years, the Dutch had kept the river Scheldt closed to trade ships, which cut the port of Antwerp off from the sea.
By 1784, Antwerp belonged to the Austrian Habsburgs, and their emperor, Joseph the Second, was sick of it.
It's a river. Rivers are for boats. I'm sending boats.
So he sent three ships down the Scheldt, including a ship called Le Louis, flying the emperor's own flag.
His logic was simple: surely the Dutch would never dare fire on the emperor's flag.
The Dutch sent out one warship, the Dolfijn.
Stop right there!
Make me.
So the Dolfijn fired.
And according to the story that gave this war its name, the one and only shot hit a soup kettle.
Not the soup!
Le Louis surrendered on the spot.
The emperor did declare war a few weeks later, but France stepped in to calm everyone down.
In the Treaty of Fontainebleau in 1785, the Scheldt stayed closed, and the Dutch paid the emperor millions of guilders to make the whole thing go away.
Total casualties: zero people, one kettle, and one lunch.
Number six is a war that supposedly lasted three hundred and thirty-five years without a single shot being fired.
And I say supposedly, because historians aren't sure this war ever really existed, so file this one under legend with paperwork.
In 1651, England was wrapping up a civil war, and some of the last Royalists were holding out on the Isles of Scilly, a tiny island chain off Cornwall.
Royalist ships had been seizing Dutch ships and cargo, so the Dutch sent Admiral Maarten Tromp to demand compensation.
Pay us back for our ships, or else!
Or else what?
According to a letter from the time, when Tromp got no satisfying answer, he said he had declared war on the islands.
A few months later, the Royalists surrendered to the English Parliament's navy anyway, and the Dutch sailed home without firing a shot.
And then everybody forgot about it, for more than three centuries.
In the mid-1980s, a local historian named Roy Duncan looked into the old story and wrote to the Dutch embassy in London.
Quick question: are we still at war with you?
Embassy staff checked, and they couldn't find a peace treaty anywhere.
So the Dutch ambassador, Rein Huydecoper, visited the islands, and on the seventeenth of April 1986, peace was officially declared.
The ambassador joked about the terror the islanders must have lived with.

show.text: …to know we could have attacked at any moment.
show.who: Dutch ambassador Rein Huydecoper, joking at the 1986 peace ceremony

beats.say: Skeptics point out that an admiral isn't a country and Scilly was part of England, so it was probably never a real war. But it was a great excuse for a party.
Number five: the War of the Bucket, northern Italy, 1325.
Modena and Bologna are two cities about twenty-five miles apart, and in the thirteen hundreds they could not stand each other.
Bologna backed the Pope, Modena backed the Holy Roman Emperor, and the border between them was basically one long argument.
Now, the legend goes like this: some soldiers from Modena snuck into Bologna and stole a wooden bucket from the town well.
Give us back our bucket!
What bucket?
And that, supposedly, started a war.
Here's the twist: that part is mostly a myth.
The real trigger was that Modena grabbed an important Bolognese castle called Monteveglio in September 1325.
So in November, Bologna marched out with an army of around thirty-two thousand men, against about seven thousand from Modena.

show.label: Battle of Zappolino, 1325
show.sub: from Bologna, against about 7,000 from Modena

beats.say: Easy win for Bologna, right?
Nope. Modena had professional German soldiers sent by the emperor, while the giant Bolognese army was mostly untrained.
The Battle of Zappolino was over within a couple of hours, and the Bolognese were routed.
For the people who were there, this was no joke: around two thousand men lost their lives.
On the way home, the Modenese took a bucket from a well just outside one of Bologna's gates, as a trophy.
We'll just take this, thanks.
They even held a victory race right outside Bologna's walls, just to rub it in.
And the bucket? Modena still has it. The original sits in the town hall, and a replica hangs in the city's famous bell tower.
Seven hundred years later, and they are still not giving it back.
Number four: the War of Jenkins' Ear, which is a real name that real historians use, I promise.
It's April 1731, and a British captain named Robert Jenkins is sailing his ship, the Rebecca, home from Jamaica.
A Spanish coast guard ship stops him on suspicion of smuggling, and to be fair, historians say his ship really was a smuggler.
The Spanish crew roughed him up, and one of them cut off his ear.
Here, take this back to your King George.
Wait, you're giving me my ear back?
Yep. One newspaper report from 1731 says they handed him the piece of his ear and told him to take it to the king.
Jenkins made it home and took his complaint to the royal court, and then, well, nothing much happened for seven years.
By 1738, British merchants were furious about Spanish ships searching their vessels, and the politicians who wanted war with Spain needed a mascot.
Enter Jenkins' ear.
The famous story says Jenkins went before a committee of Parliament and showed them his ear, pickled in a jar.
Gentlemen, I brought the ear.
Why would you keep it?
Some historians say there's no solid evidence for that dramatic jar scene, but the story spread like wildfire anyway.
Prime Minister Robert Walpole didn't want a war, but the pressure was too much, and in 1739 Britain declared war on Spain.
A war. Over an ear.
And this one was not small.
The biggest British attack, on Cartagena in South America in 1741, was a disaster with heavy losses.
The fighting soon merged into a much bigger European war, the War of the Austrian Succession, and only formally ended in 1748.
Britain mostly failed to get what it wanted, and the most famous thing about the whole war is still one man's ear.
Number three is the shortest war in recorded history.
Zanzibar, an island off the coast of East Africa, in August 1896.
Zanzibar had a sultan but was a British protectorate, and the deal said any new sultan needed British approval.
On the twenty-fifth of August, the pro-British sultan died suddenly, and Khalid bin Barghash moved into the palace and took the throne without asking.
I'm the sultan now.
The British wanted someone else, so they sent an ultimatum: take down your flag and leave the palace by nine in the morning on the twenty-seventh, or we open fire.
Leave by nine, or we fire.
You wouldn't dare.
Around two thousand eight hundred defenders barricaded themselves in and around the palace, while five British warships lined up in the harbor.
Nine o'clock came. At two minutes past nine, the ships opened fire.
By about twenty to ten, the palace flag had been shot down, and it was over.
Now, the length is the ridiculous part, but the war itself was not a joke.
Around five hundred people on Khalid's side were killed or wounded, many of them when the palace caught fire, while on the British side one sailor was injured.
Khalid escaped to the German consulate and was later carried off on a German warship.
And then came the coldest part: Britain made Khalid's supporters pay for the shells that had been fired at them, plus damages from looting.
Number two: the Pig War, and yes, there is a pig.
In 1859, the United States and Britain both claimed San Juan Island, which sits between today's Washington State and Vancouver Island in Canada.
A treaty said the border ran down the middle of the channel, but there were two channels, and the island sat right between them.
On the fifteenth of June 1859, an American farmer named Lyman Cutlar found a pig rooting around in his garden.
And it was not the first time.
Not again!
So he shot it.
The pig belonged to Charles Griffin, who ran a sheep farm on the island for Britain's Hudson's Bay Company.
Cutlar offered ten dollars. Griffin wanted a hundred.
There's a story, probably made up, that the two men had this exchange.
It was eating my potatoes!
Then keep your potatoes out of my pig!
When British officials threatened to arrest Cutlar, the American settlers asked the U.S. Army for protection.
The Army sent Captain George Pickett with sixty-four soldiers.
Nobody is arresting anybody on this island.
Britain answered with warships, and by the end of August there were four hundred sixty-one American soldiers and fourteen cannons on the island.

show.label: San Juan Island, August 1859
show.sub: US soldiers, facing British warships with over 2,000 men

beats.say: All over one dead pig.
Luckily, the British naval commander in the Pacific, Rear Admiral Robert Baynes, took one look and refused to start shooting.
He told the local governor he would not do this.

show.text: Involve two great nations in a war over a squabble about a pig.

beats.say: Meanwhile, on the island, things got weirdly friendly: officers from both sides went to church together and shared whisky and cigars.
The two countries agreed to share the island, and that joint military occupation lasted twelve years.
Finally, the question went to Germany's Kaiser Wilhelm the First, and in 1872 his arbitration commission gave the islands to the United States.
Final body count of the Pig War: one pig.
And number one. You knew it was coming. The Great Emu War.
After World War One, Australia gave thousands of veterans land to farm in Western Australia, often pretty marginal land.
Then the Great Depression hit, wheat prices kept falling, and in 1932 an estimated twenty thousand emus showed up.
Emus migrate after breeding season, and these ones discovered that farms had water, cleared land and lots of delicious wheat.
Lunch is served, boys.
Many of the farmers were ex-soldiers, and they knew exactly what works against a big advancing army: machine guns.
Minister, we need machine guns.
For the birds?
For the birds.
Defence Minister Sir George Pearce said yes.
So the army sent Major Meredith of the Royal Australian Artillery, two soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and ten thousand rounds of ammunition.
They even brought along a newsreel cameraman to film the big victory.
The operation started on the second of November 1932.
The first flock of about fifty emus was out of range, so local settlers tried to herd them into an ambush.
The emus split into small groups and ran in every direction.
Why won't they stay in formation?
Two days later, Meredith set up an ambush near a dam, and more than a thousand emus came heading straight for his guns.
This was it. The gunners waited until the birds were close, and opened fire.
After about a dozen birds, the gun jammed.
And the rest of the flock scattered.
Meredith then mounted a gun on a truck, but the truck couldn't keep up, and the ride was so rough the gunner couldn't fire a single shot.
Army observers even reported that each pack seemed to have its own leader, a big black-plumed bird about six feet tall, keeping watch while the others ate.
Humans incoming. Scatter!
Within a week, about two and a half thousand rounds had been fired, and estimates of birds killed range from fifty to five hundred.
Meredith noted that his men had suffered no casualties. Their pride was another story.
The newspapers had a field day, and on the eighth of November the soldiers were pulled out.
But the emus kept eating, the farmers kept complaining, and within a week the army was back.
The second round went a bit better, and by early December they were killing around a hundred emus a week.
When Meredith was recalled on the tenth of December, he claimed nine hundred eighty-six kills, plus two and a half thousand wounded birds, a figure that's highly disputed.
But his verdict on his feathered enemy became legendary.

show.text: If we had a military division with the bullet-carrying capacity of these birds it would face any army in the world… They can face machine guns with the invulnerability of tanks.
show.who: Major G.P.W. Meredith, as reported in the press

beats.say: Farmers asked for the army again in 1934, 1943 and 1948, and the government said no every time.
In the end, bounties and big fences did the job the machine guns couldn't.
So the final score reads: emus one, machine guns zero.
So there you have it: a kettle, a legend, a bucket, an ear, a very short war, a pig, and an army that got outrun by birds.
If there's one lesson here, it's that humans will start a war over almost anything, and sometimes the other side has feathers.
Next up: Mansa Musa, the richest man who ever lived. See you there.

description:
A pig, a bucket, a soup kettle, a sailor's ear and twenty thousand emus: these are the most ridiculous wars in history, counted down from seven to one. Six of them definitely happened, one might be a legend with paperwork, and yes, that includes the one where the Australian army lost a fight with birds. Chapters are added automatically.
